title: Rivers of living water (John 7:37–39)
hookLine: on the feast's last day he stands and cries out

lines: ON THE LAST DAY, HE SHOUTS.
cards: Autumn in Jerusalem, and the city is full of huts. For the feast of Tabernacles, families build shelters of branches on rooftops and in courtyards and live in them for a week, remembering the years in the desert.
It's a harvest festival, and a prayer for rain before the dry ground has to be planted.
Each morning of the feast, according to the old Jewish sources, a priest carried water up from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it out at the altar, with trumpets and singing.
On the last day, the great day, Jesus stands up and shouts.

teach.b: John says he stood and cried out, a man on his feet, raising his voice over a festival crowd.
In the Douay-Rheims: "If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink."
Then: "He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith, Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Out of his belly sounds strange in English.
The Greek word means the belly, the inside, the deepest part of a person; we'd say the heart, or the gut. We've heard living water before, at the well in Samaria. Here it isn't a cup.

teach.h: THIS HE SAID OF THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: And John stops to tell us what it means: this he said of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive; the Spirit wasn't yet given, because Jesus wasn't yet glorified.
So the water poured at the altar becomes a picture of something still to come. Here's an old puzzle: the sentence can be divided two ways. The Douay reads it as the believer's belly.
But some early Christian writers read it as Christ's own: let the one who believes come and drink, for out of him flow rivers.
Both readings have histories in the Church, and some readers hear them together: the Spirit flows from Christ, and then through the believer to others. John may be pointing ahead, too.
At the cross, a soldier's spear opens Jesus's side, and blood and water come out. The Catechism sees the sacraments, and the Church itself, flowing from that wound.

how: Catholics hear John 7:37–39 at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, linking the rivers of living water to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

games.q: what does “rivers of living water” mean?
o: water drawn from Siloam for the altar
the Spirit flowing out from within
the Jordan where John baptized crowds

games.q: on the great day — tap the pairs.
p: a week in huts of branches
drawn at Siloam, poured at the altar
the inside, the heart of a person

s: Jesus said this quietly to his disciples
he stood and cried out on the last, great day of the feast.
John explains that the living water means the Spirit
this he said of the Spirit, which believers would receive.
every Bible agrees whose belly the rivers flow from
the sentence can be divided two ways: the believer's belly, or Christ's.

games.q: it's the last day of a festival about water and harvest. the priests have poured water at the altar every morning. you're a teacher in the crowd. what do you do?
o: sit and teach a small group quietly.
stand up and cry out: if any man thirst, come to me.
leave before the crowds get too big.
games.why: he stood and cried: if any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink. out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.

practice: Breathe in and notice something you've been given lately, a kindness, rest, an idea, time; breathe out slowly and picture some of it flowing on, past you, to someone else, because a river doesn't keep its water.
If you pray, ask that what you've been given flow out; if not, just let one person come to mind who could use it.

wordCard.voice: Rivers of living water. Jesus's cry on the last day of Tabernacles; John says he meant the Spirit, flowing out of the one who believes. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: belly, the inmost part of a person (John 7:38).

carryVoice: Your line: out of his belly. Not a cup of water, but rivers. See you tomorrow.
